newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian oil town calm after army moves in.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian oil town calm after army moves in.

text.p: The Nigerian oil town of Warri where communal fighting has raged for a month was peaceful on Thursday following the deployment of troops there, residents and the military command said.
"It is calm and people are going about their businesses like before," said a hotel manager reached by telephone in Warri, 300 kms (190 miles) east of Lagos in the midwestern Delta state.
Defence headquarters spokesman Colonel Godwin Ugbo said soldiers sent into the town on Tuesday night had quickly succeeded in restoring order.
"The situation in Warri is under control and reports we have is that the people are happy themselves that the soldiers are there," he told Reuters in Lagos.
The deployment of troops followed clashes between armed youths over the transfer of the local council headquarters from an Ijaw town to that of the rival Itsekiri tribe.
The fighting resulted in the death of more than 65 people from both sides, including police personnel who became powerless to control gangs of armed youth.

At the height of the crisis in March, armed Ijaw tribesmen occupied six oil-flow stations of the Nigerian unit of Royal Dutch Shell Group, shutting off 100,000 barrels per day of its crude oil production.
Some 127 of Shell's Nigerian staff held by the tribesmen were released after negotiations and oil output resumed.
Ugbo said soldiers would remain in Warri until "when peace is fully guaranteed."
"We don't usually move the military into internal wranglings until we consider the situation beyond the control of the police," he said.
At the root of the crisis is a long-standing rivalry among three tribes -- the Ijaws, the Itsekiris and the Urhobos.
